title: Google, NVIDIA and Emerald AI Launch Power-Flexibility Coalition for Data Centers
excerpt: The AI Energy Management Alliance brings AI labs, chipmakers and utilities together to push demand flexibility and grid-reliability standards for AI data centers.
body:
• Google, NVIDIA and Emerald AI have founded the AI Energy Management Alliance (AEMA) to promote flexible AI data centers that act as assets on the power grid rather than strains on it.
  • Inaugural members span the full AI-to-grid value chain, including Anthropic, Constellation, National Grid, NRG, RWE and 14 other energy and technology firms, with energy executive Frank Lacey as executive director.
  • The coalition will push for technology-neutral, performance-based standards that measure data centers on grid reliability — aiming for faster AI deployment without asking ratepayers to fund new capacity.

Google, NVIDIA and Emerald AI on Tuesday launched the AI Energy Management Alliance (AEMA), a new coalition to make AI data centers flexible participants on the power grid — able to shift and throttle their enormous electricity demand as grid conditions change.

The alliance, which evolves from the Advanced Energy Management Alliance founded in 2014, convenes AI platforms, infrastructure firms, data center operators, utilities and grid operators under one roof. Its founding pitch is that intelligent energy management can turn data centers from a looming strain on electricity systems into assets that help them run more reliably and affordably.

Who is in — and what they want

Joining the three founders as inaugural members and launch partners are AES, Analog Devices, Anthropic, Calibrant Energy, Camus, ClearPath, Constellation, Encoord, Fluence, Generate Capital, GridUnity, National Grid, NRG, PassKey, RWE, Splight, Verrus and Voltus. Frank Lacey, a veteran energy industry executive, will serve as executive director.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=m518bhzjU5A

The coalition's central policy ask is for technology-neutral, performance-based standards that evaluate flexible data centers on measurable grid reliability metrics, rather than prescribing how they manage their power. AEMA's members are also pushing demand flexibility — scheduling and shifting the energy-intensive computing work, like AI model training, to off-peak periods — as a way to unlock faster connections to the grid while protecting affordability for ordinary energy consumers.

Why it matters now

The timing reflects the scale of the AI power crunch. Data centers supporting AI training and inference draw power at unprecedented densities — industry estimates point to rack densities reaching 600 kilowatts as next-generation AI chips arrive — and utilities across the United States are fielding connection requests that outstrip available capacity. That bottleneck has become one of the main constraints on how fast AI infrastructure can be built.

Flexible data centers offer a way to build faster without building as much new generation: if a data center can ramp down during grid stress and ramp up when electricity is abundant, it imposes less strain at peak moments and can connect sooner.

The fastest path to reliable, affordable energy is making smarter use of what already exists, even as we build the new infrastructure we need. — Josh Parker, Head of Sustainability, NVIDIA

The quotes behind the launch

"Google is committed to investing in energy solutions that benefit everyone, and pioneering smarter ways to manage our demand turns data centers into dynamic grid allies that help power systems operate more efficiently and reliably," said Tyler Norris, Google's head of advanced energy market innovation.

"The fastest path to reliable, affordable energy is making smarter use of what already exists, even as we build the new infrastructure we need," said Josh Parker, NVIDIA's head of sustainability. "NVIDIA is joining AEMA to advocate for technology-neutral, performance-based standards that evaluate flexible data centers on measurable grid reliability metrics. The result: faster AI deployment and a more efficient grid, without asking ratepayers to fund new capacity."

What to watch next

The coalition's first test will be whether regulators and utilities adopt its proposed standards framework — and whether flexible-operation pledges translate into actual grid relief rather than marketing language. Anthropic's presence alongside NVIDIA and Google also signals that the AI labs themselves see power access, not just chips, as the binding constraint on the next phase of the AI buildout. The group's policy positions and member endorsements are posted at aema.ai.
